Awakateko

Awakateko people have their principal homeland around Aguacatán in Huehuetenango, Guatemala, with communities also established in Mexico. Their Maya language is called Qa'yool or Qyool in Mexican sources. Community-led language research, school materials and migration histories reveal an identity rooted in a particular highland region while extending across national borders.

Names & relationshipsAwakateko is a particular Maya people and language, closely related linguistically to Ixil. It is distinct from Akateko despite the similar spelling. The ALMG linguistic community is a language institution, not a government over every Awakateko community.
An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
01

Names and a highland homeland

Mexico's Indigenous-peoples atlas records qatanum, meaning our people, as a self-designation and explains Awakateko through the place name Aguacatán. The community's own linguistic atlas locates its homeland at the foot of the Sierra de los Cuchumatanes. Awakateko is one of several distinct Maya languages, rather than another word for Maya as a whole. Its close linguistic relationship with Ixil should also be distinguished from the similarly spelled Akateko, a different language and people in this directory.

Read the sources [1] Instituto Nacional de los Pueblos Indígenas [2] Comunidad Lingüística Awakateka / Academia de las Lenguas Mayas de Guatemala, with CIESAS and CIMSUR-UNAM [3] Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas

02

Displacement and communities in Mexico

INALI connects the Awakateko presence in Mexico with flight from Guatemala's civil war and military repression. Its migration account describes the relocation of Guatemalan Indigenous communities to different Mexican states in 1984–1985, followed by further movement for work, including to the United States. A newer INALI profile specifically identifies Maya Tecún I, Maya Tecún II and Santo Domingo Kesté in Champotón, Campeche. These settlements belong to a transnational history; migration does not make Aguacatán the only legitimate location of Awakateko life.

Read the sources [4] Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas [3] Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas

03

Work, clothing and adaptation

The INPI ethnography describes garlic and onion cultivation, seasonal crops, sheep raising, weaving, professional employment and agricultural migration. Its discussion of women's clothing identifies embroidered huipiles, woven skirts and sashes as forms of cultural expression. These are examples within a changing community, not a dress requirement or a complete occupational portrait. The same account notes adaptation of plant knowledge after settlement in Chiapas and Campeche, where different climates and vegetation created new conditions for everyday life.

Read the sources [1] Instituto Nacional de los Pueblos Indígenas

04

Hearing local variation directly

The Atlas Lingüístico Sonoro del Awakateko is led by the Comunidad Lingüística Awakateka within Guatemala's Maya-language academy, with advice from CIESAS and CIMSUR-UNAM. Its first version compares 400 entries from nine Aguacatán communities through maps, recordings and practical and phonetic transcriptions. Two speakers represent each location. Differences occur in sounds, word forms and vocabulary, sometimes within one community. This direct evidence shows why INALI's single catalogued Mexican variety should not be read as proof that everyone speaks identically.

Read the sources [2] Comunidad Lingüística Awakateka / Academia de las Lenguas Mayas de Guatemala, with CIESAS and CIMSUR-UNAM [3] Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas

05

Teaching and community authorship

In June 2025, Guatemala's government news agency reported the distribution of approximately 2,050 copies of Literatura Maya: Principios y Valores Culturales Awakateko to schools in Aguacatán. The Comunidad Lingüística Awakateka coordinated with educational authorities, reaching institutions at several school levels. Alongside its sound atlas and earlier grammars, this work places community knowledge into learning materials. It also changes the research perspective: Awakateko speakers are authors, investigators and teachers, rather than merely subjects counted in endangered-language statistics.

Read the sources [5] Agencia Guatemalteca de Noticias [2] Comunidad Lingüística Awakateka / Academia de las Lenguas Mayas de Guatemala, with CIESAS and CIMSUR-UNAM
